questions.q: 4-Bromotoluene is treated with sodium in dry ether. The main coupling product is:
questions.explain: In the Fittig reaction two aryl halides join where the halogens were, and ring substituents stay in place, so two para-tolyl groups are linked at C-4.

questions.q: Which combination of reactants, each treated with Na in dry ether, gives toluene?
questions.explain: One aryl halide plus one alkyl halide with Na/dry ether is the Wurtz–Fittig reaction, which gives an alkylarene Ar–R. Bromobenzene alone (Fittig) gives biphenyl and bromomethane alone (Wurtz) gives ethane.

questions.q: Alkyl halides couple with sodium more readily than aryl halides (Wurtz faster than Fittig). The main reason is that the aryl C–X bond:
options: is weaker because the aryl carbon is sp³
is non-polar because the ring withdraws electrons
has partial double-bond character from resonance and involves an sp² carbon
cannot form radicals under any conditions
questions.explain: Resonance gives the aryl C–X bond partial double-bond character and the carbon is sp², so the bond is stronger and harder to break. Aryl radicals do form, though,, as shown by triphenylene in the product mixture.

questions.q: A mixture of chlorobenzene and 4-chlorotoluene is treated with sodium in dry ether. How many different biaryls can be expected?
questions.explain: Two different aryl groups can couple as Ar–Ar, Ar′–Ar′ and Ar–Ar′, giving three biaryls. This is why the Fittig reaction is used only for symmetrical biaryls.
